newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Nat Express/Schoyen plan Euro expansion.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Nat Express/Schoyen plan Euro expansion.

text.p: British rail-to-bus giant National Express Plc and Schoyen Group, one of Norway's biggest bus operators, revealed its joint venture plans to launch an expansion drive across Europe.

The joint venture company Concordia Bus, in which l be 63-percent held by National Express the senior partner with a 63 percent stake. It aims to exploit the huge opportunities in continental Europe as countries there seek to follow the transport deregulation and privatisation seen in Britain over the last 10 years.
The deal marks the beginning of National Express realising a long-stated ambition to conquer Continental markets after becoming a dominant force at home in rail and buses.

Phil White, chief executive of the British group, said the JV would not just bid for public transport contracts but would be primarily a vehicle for acquisitions of other bus operators in the Nordic and Baltic regions and Germany.
"We plan to make some fairly chunky acquisitions," he told Reuters.
He refused to say how much cash had been ploughed into the JV but said it was small at this stage. The real spending begins once acquisition targets have been lined up.
White added that National Express had "a lot of flexibility to gear up" with its gearing ratio a mere three percent.
Concordia will aim to buy major bus operators with more than 500 buses apiece and those running in urban areas.
"Schoyen has already identified some acquisition targets. We will aim for large operators in cities," said White in the interview.
Asked when the first acquisition through Concordia could be expected, he said it might not happen in 1997 but that he "would be disappointed if we did not have at least one underway in 1998."
Concordia will be chaired by Schoyen President Frode Larsen with White as the deputy chairman. It will have three National Express directors and two from the Norwegian company.

White sees National Express' experience of British transport deregulation and privatisation as a key factor in winning deals on the Continent as it too goes down that route due to domestic budgetary constraints.
"The private sector is set to play an increasingly important role throughout Europe," said White.
"National Express' experience of operating in the highly competitive, deregulated UK transport sector combined with Schoyen's local expertise will make Concordia a powerful force," he concluded.
But for now, shares remain unexcited, down two and a half pence at 492 1/2 pence per share.
Analysts viewed the venture as a cautious first step.
"It is a stepping stone and one must examine what kind of deal eventually comes out of it," said Andrew Darke at Williams de Brose.
"It is important to either get it right first time with a European acquisition, as Stagecoach did with Swebus, or link up with a very good local partner," he added.
The British group's new partner is a broad-based transport operator which provides 40 percent of Oslo's bus services and employs 800 staff.
National Express sees Concordia as a blueprint for European expansion in other sectors like rail.
But White disagreed that the number of British transport operators looking for strategic alliances in Europe was likely to inflate the cost of such deals.

Almost every major British transport group is looking for a Continental deal to act as a springboard for expansion. Stagecoach Plc saw its shares rocket last year when it bought the Swedish bus group Swebus.
Go-Ahead Group Plc and FirstBus Plc have also been seeking a similar type of entry point.
